take: Brent January climbed 1.3% as renewed Middle East supply threats outweighed surplus concerns, with Standard Chartered arguing oil needs a fresh shock to fall further, whilst EIA data showing collective chokepoint flows up 19% in 3Q26 underscores how much of the marginal barrel still transits those routes. The hawkish Fed poised to raise rates despite stock market turmoil is the macro thread to pull, since tighter US policy lifts the dollar and squeezes EM demand just as gasoline softens into Thanksgiving (national average falling sharply in November) whilst diesel stays expensive, keeping the gasoline-diesel spread wide and refining margins skewed to middle distillates. Inventory and positioning cues are thin today, but the US-Venezuela crude import surge to 701,000 b/d in July before easing to 655,000 b/d in August is worth tracking as heavy-sour replacement flow, and Alaska's forecast 13% production growth in 2027 (a 23,000 b/d rise) adds a slow-burn medium-term supply offset. The cross-market link sits in products: cheap gasoline against stubborn diesel normalises the crack structure toward distillate, which feeds directly into bunker economics and tonne-miles as owners weigh scrubber economics against VLSFO spreads. Watch the dollar reaction to Fed rhetoric and any further Libya escalation around Benghazi, since both transmit straight into Brent flat price and freight risk premia within the next 24 hours.

items.title: U.S. natural gas inventories end injection season above normal levels
items.summary: Working natural gas in storage in the Lower 48 states ended the natural gas injection season at 3,810 billion cubic feet (Bcf), exceeding the five-year average by almost 2%, according to estimates based on data from our Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report released on November 12. Injection season runs April 1–October 31, the months of typically lower natural gas demand.

items.title: EIA forecasts Alaskan crude oil production to grow 13% in 2027
items.summary: After decades of decline, crude oil production in Alaska is growing, driven by two projects on Alaska's North Slope. In our latest Short-Term Energy Outlook, we expect a 23,000 barrels per day (b/d) (6%) increase in 2026, followed by a 60,000 b/d (13%) rise in 2027. At a forecast 505,000 b/d in 2027, output would be the most since 2014.
